entries.meaning: Adds another important supporting point in an argument.
entries.example: The new library is easy to reach. Furthermore, it has free study rooms.
entries.note: Often begins a new sentence followed by a comma.
entries.common_error: Do not join independent sentences with only a comma before furthermore.

entries.meaning: Adds a second point that strengthens the previous one.
entries.example: The class project is inexpensive. Moreover, it uses recycled materials.
entries.note: Usually followed by a comma at the start of a sentence.
entries.common_error: Do not add it where the second idea merely repeats the first.

entries.meaning: Introduces an extra piece of relevant information.
entries.example: The workshop teaches photography. Additionally, students can practise editing.
entries.note: Use a comma after an initial linking adverb.
entries.common_error: Not a direct conjunction between two clauses without suitable punctuation.

entries.meaning: Adds another comparable activity or item.
entries.example: The club teaches painting as well as drawing.
entries.note: Often joins noun or -ing phrases; agreement may follow the main subject rather than the added phrase.
entries.common_error: Do not automatically use it to join two independent sentences.
entries.construction: noun phrase + as well as + noun phrase (or -ing phrase)

entries.meaning: Offers a further, often conversational, reason.
entries.example: We can walk to the park. Besides, the weather is lovely.
entries.note: Sentence-initial besides commonly takes a comma.
entries.common_error: Do not confuse besides (in addition) with beside (next to).

entries.meaning: Adds precise facts that strengthen or correct an earlier impression.
entries.example: Some students expected a difficult quiz. In fact, it was quite short.
entries.note: The second sentence should genuinely clarify the first.
entries.common_error: Do not use in fact to introduce an unrelated opinion.

entries.meaning: Presents a different side of the same topic or decision.
entries.example: Online lessons are flexible. On the other hand, group discussion can be harder.
entries.note: Use when comparing two meaningful perspectives.
entries.common_error: Do not use for every small contrast that is already clear with but.
entries.construction: One side or advantage. On the other hand, + another side

entries.meaning: Signals an outcome that holds despite the preceding obstacle.
entries.example: The route was difficult. Nevertheless, the hikers finished safely.
entries.note: Commonly sentence-initial with a comma.
entries.common_error: Avoid a comma splice between two independent clauses.

entries.meaning: Signals that the following claim still holds despite a difficulty.
entries.example: The plan needs more time. Nonetheless, it deserves consideration.
entries.note: Closely overlaps nevertheless; formality and context matter.
entries.common_error: Do not imply there is a major obstacle when none has been stated.
entries.construction: Obstacle or limitation. Nonetheless, + contrasting claim

entries.meaning: Compares contrasting facts within a complex sentence.
entries.example: Whereas my sister enjoys history, I prefer geography.
entries.note: The opening whereas-clause is commonly followed by a comma.
entries.common_error: Do not use whereas + noun phrase in place of a finite clause here.

entries.meaning: Can contrast two facts or preferences.
entries.example: While I prefer printed books, my brother reads on a tablet.
entries.note: While can also mean during the time that; context decides.
entries.common_error: Do not assume every use of while expresses contrast.

entries.meaning: Highlights a somewhat surprising contrast.
entries.example: Even though the bus was late, we reached the museum on time.
entries.note: The initial subordinate clause is usually separated by a comma.
entries.common_error: Avoid 'even though ..., but ...' as a double connector in one construction.
entries.construction: Even though + finite clause, + main clause

entries.meaning: Introduces a consequence supported by an earlier cause.
entries.example: It snowed overnight. As a result, the match was postponed.
entries.note: As a result of + noun phrase is a different construction.
entries.common_error: Do not present an unsupported guess as a proven result.
entries.construction: Cause sentence. As a result, + outcome sentence

entries.meaning: Marks a logical consequence in a formal explanation.
entries.example: The measurements were inaccurate. Consequently, the experiment was repeated.
entries.note: Often followed by a comma when used at sentence start.
entries.common_error: Not a substitute for however, which expresses contrast.

entries.meaning: Joins a cause to its result within a sentence.
entries.example: The classroom was hot, so we opened the windows.
entries.note: A comma is common when so joins two independent clauses.
entries.common_error: Avoid 'because it was hot, so we opened the windows' in a standard single construction.

entries.meaning: Introduces a particular illustration of a broader point.
entries.example: Some activities improve concentration. For instance, a short walk can help.
entries.note: Often functions much like for example.
entries.common_error: An illustration is not proof that every case behaves the same way.
entries.construction: General point. For instance, + specific example

entries.meaning: Narrows a broad statement to an exact detail or requirement.
entries.example: Our plan needs clearer steps. Specifically, we must agree on the deadline.
entries.note: Use it when providing more precision, not necessarily a new example.
entries.common_error: Do not use it to introduce information unrelated to the general statement.

entries.meaning: Highlights one important member or detail within a broader set.
entries.example: Several clubs need supplies. In particular, the art club needs paint.
entries.note: Can appear in other sentence positions with suitable punctuation.
entries.common_error: Do not use it to introduce something not included in the original set.
entries.construction: General statement. In particular, + highlighted item

entries.meaning: Signals a parallel action, feature, or outcome.
entries.example: The first group checked its sources. Likewise, the second group verified the facts.
entries.note: Needs a meaningful similarity, not simply the next event.
entries.common_error: Do not confuse similarity with cause-and-effect.
entries.construction: Sentence A. Likewise, + parallel sentence B

entries.meaning: Introduces something comparable in the relevant respect.
entries.example: Some students learn well from diagrams. Similarly, others benefit from visual examples.
entries.note: Explain what makes the two cases alike when the relationship is not obvious.
entries.common_error: Do not use if the examples differ in the very feature being compared.

entries.meaning: Directly highlights a difference between two things.
entries.example: The main road is busy. In contrast, the side street is quiet.
entries.note: Choose comparable points of reference.
entries.common_error: Do not use if there is no real difference to contrast.
entries.construction: Situation A. In contrast, + situation B

entries.meaning: Indicates an alternative that replaces a previous possibility.
entries.example: We did not take the bus. Instead, we walked to the science museum.
entries.note: May also appear before a verb phrase or at sentence end.
entries.common_error: Not interchangeable with however when nothing was replaced.

entries.meaning: Means approximately 'if not' in this conditional use.
entries.example: Bring your student card. Otherwise, you may need to pay the full price.
entries.note: Make sure the implied negative condition is easy to identify.
entries.common_error: Do not treat otherwise as a general word for contrast.
entries.construction: Instruction or condition. Otherwise, + possible result

entries.meaning: Normally expresses an exception: if the condition does not happen.
entries.example: Unless it rains, we will practise outside.
entries.note: Unless it rains is similar in meaning to if it does not rain in this example.
entries.common_error: Avoid an unnecessary extra negative in 'unless it doesn't rain' when meaning 'if it doesn't rain'.

entries.meaning: Adds a condition that must be met.
entries.example: You may borrow the camera provided that you return it tomorrow.
entries.note: Often used when permission or agreement depends on a condition.
entries.common_error: Do not mistake provided that for the past participle of provide in this construction.
entries.construction: Main clause + provided that + finite clause

entries.meaning: Restates an idea to make the meaning clearer.
entries.example: The activity is optional. In other words, you can decide whether to join.
entries.note: The restatement should preserve the original meaning.
entries.common_error: Do not use to add an unrelated or contradictory claim.
entries.construction: Statement A. In other words, + clearer restatement

entries.meaning: Introduces a brief summary at the end of a longer explanation.
entries.example: To sum up, our plan is affordable and gives everyone a chance to participate.
entries.note: Use a conclusion when the text genuinely needs one.
entries.common_error: Avoid adding this formula mechanically to a two-sentence answer.

entries.meaning: Highlights the most important point among several.
entries.example: We should consider cost and convenience. Above all, we must keep students safe.
entries.note: The final point should genuinely deserve priority.
entries.common_error: Not equivalent to first in a simple time sequence.
entries.construction: Several concerns. Above all, + most important one

entries.meaning: Signals the first step or first important point.
entries.example: First of all, read the instructions before using the equipment.
entries.note: Useful when several ordered steps or points follow.
entries.common_error: Do not pair it with an unrelated last point merely to sound organized.

entries.meaning: Refers to the next step after a previously described action.
entries.example: Mix the ingredients carefully. After that, pour the mixture into a tray.
entries.note: Requires a clear earlier action or event.
entries.common_error: Do not use if the second event happened before the first.
